# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Finds Its Way Up

Water is heavy. This single fact explains almost everything about how municipal water systems work. A gallon of water weighs about 8.3 pounds, and a column of water only one inch square but ten feet tall already exerts over four pounds per square inch of pressure at its base. Engineers exploit this relationship constantly, and it's the reason the first question any water utility asks about a new building isn't about plumbing—it's about elevation.

## The Fundamental Physics: Head

In the water business, engineers talk about "head" rather than pressure. Head is simply the vertical distance between the water's surface and the point where it exits a tap, expressed in feet. Every 2.31 feet of elevation produces roughly 1 psi (pound per square inch) of pressure. This conversion factor is the backbone of water system design.

Consider a hypothetical city—call it Riverton—whose main reservoir sits in hills 300 feet above the downtown core.
